title.en: Object-oriented programming: objects, classes and principles

hook.en: A school has students, teachers and classrooms, each with data (name, roll number) and things they do (attend, teach). *Object-oriented programming* builds software the same way: out of objects.

objectives.en: Define object, class, state and behaviour
Explain abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism

say.en: A school has students, teachers and classrooms, each with data (name, roll number) and things they do (attend, teach). Object-oriented programming builds software the same way: out of objects. In this lesson: Define object, class, state and behaviour.
Explain abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
Compare procedure-oriented and object-oriented programming.

body.en: An object is an entity with a state (its data, held in fields or instance variables) and behaviour (what it can do, its methods). A class is the blueprint, or template, from which *objects* are created; each object is an instance of a class. One class Student can produce many Student objects, each with its own name and roll number but the same methods. Objects interact by sending messages, that is, by calling each other's methods.

title.en: On the board: the four principles of OOP

say.en: Object-oriented programming rests on four ideas.
Abstraction: show only what matters and hide the details. You drive a car without knowing its engine.
Encapsulation: wrap data and the methods that use it into one unit, the class, and hide the data from outside (private).
Inheritance: a new class reuses and extends an existing class. A Car is a kind of Vehicle.
Polymorphism: one name, many forms. The same method call behaves differently for different objects.

body.en: In *procedure-oriented* programming (as in C or BASIC) a program is a list of functions working on shared data; data moves freely and is easy to damage. In object-oriented programming (Java, C++, Python) data and the functions on it are bundled into objects, the data is hidden (data hiding), and code is reused through classes and inheritance. OOP programs are organised bottom-up, from objects to the whole system.

points.en: OOP favours reuse and bottom-up design

problem.en: Identify the class, two attributes and two behaviours for a library book system, and write the class skeleton in Java.

steps.en: class Book { String title; int accessionNo; boolean isIssued; void issue() { isIssued = true; } void giveBack() { isIssued = false; } }

answer.en: Book has state (title, accessionNo, isIssued) and behaviour (issue, giveBack).

say.en: Identify the class, two attributes and two behaviours for a library book system, and write the class skeleton in Java.
Class: Book.
Attributes state: title, accessionNo, isIssued.
Behaviours methods: issue(), giveBack().
class Book { String title; int accessionNo; boolean isIssued; void issue() { isIssued equals true; } void giveBack() { isIssued equals false; } }.
So the answer is Book has state (title, accessionNo, isIssued) and behaviour (issue, giveBack).
